parts.contextVi: Một người đàn ông gọi điện đến trung tâm cộng đồng để hỏi và đăng ký khóa học làm gốm.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Good morning, Willowbrook Community Centre, Megan speaking. How can I help?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Hello. I saw a poster for your beginners' pottery course, and I'd like to find out about joining it.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Of course. We still have places on the autumn course. Can I take your details first? What's your surname?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: It's Brenton.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Could you spell that for me, please?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Sure. That's B-R-E-N-T-O-N.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Thank you, Mr Brenton. And a contact number?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: My mobile is oh one six one, five five five, oh one four seven.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Lovely. Now, the course runs on three evenings, Tuesday, Wednesday or Thursday. Which would suit you?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Tuesday would be best, because I finish work early that day.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Oh, I'm sorry, the Tuesday class is already full. Wednesday has places, and so does Thursday.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: I play football on Wednesdays, so Thursday it is.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Great. The poster says the class starts at seven o'clock, but we've changed it, so it's seven fifteen and finishes at nine thirty.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: And how much is the course?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: It used to be seventy-five pounds, but the price went up this term, so it's eighty-five pounds for ten weeks, including all the clay.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: That's fine. Do I need to bring anything?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Just an apron, as clay gets everywhere. All the tools are provided, and you don't need a towel because there are sinks in the studio.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Where exactly is the centre?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: We're on Mill Lane, just past the post office.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: And is there somewhere to park?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: The small car park at the front is for staff, and the street opposite the café is always busy. Most people use the car park behind the library, which is only a two-minute walk.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Good. And which room is the class in?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Studio twelve, on the first floor. Studio two on the ground floor is for the painting class, so please don't go there by mistake.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: One more thing. Are there any discounts?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Yes, pensioners get ten percent off, but unfortunately students don't. I'll send you a confirmation by email. Thanks for calling, Mr Brenton.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Thank you very much. Goodbye.

parts.title: Welcome to Kestrel Valley Nature Park
parts.contextVi: Một nhân viên công viên giới thiệu cho du khách về lịch sử, giờ mở cửa, bản đồ và sự kiện của công viên thiên nhiên.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Good morning everyone, and welcome to Kestrel Valley Nature Park. Before you set off, I'll give you a quick introduction. The park is only twenty-five years old, but the land has a long history. Many people assume it was farmland, and some of the stone walls do come from old farms, but most of the lake was actually created when a quarry was flooded after the stone workers left in the nineteen seventies.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Opening times are worth knowing. The car park opens at eight, for walkers and dog owners, but the visitor centre, where you can pick up maps, doesn't open until nine. The café opens even later, at ten, so you might want to bring a snack if you arrive early.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Entry to the park is free, and so is parking, which surprises many visitors. The only thing you pay for is our guided walks, which are six pounds per person and last about ninety minutes. Bird-watching and walking on the main paths cost nothing at all.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Now let me take you round the map. The first aid point is right next to the main gate, so you'll pass it as you come in. The café used to be in the visitor centre, but it moved last year, and it's now inside the old barn, the stone building you can see in the middle of the map.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: The toilets are behind the visitor centre, not in it, which confuses a lot of people, so look for the small wooden building. If you're keen on birds, many visitors expect the hide to be along the river path, but the best one is actually beside the lake, so head there early in the morning.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: If you'd like to explore on two wheels, bike hire is run by a separate company, and you'll find it at the south entrance, which is the opposite end of the park from the main gate. It's about a twenty-minute walk from here, so you may prefer to drive round.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: A few requests before you go. Dogs are welcome but must be kept on a lead because of the nesting birds, and you're welcome to take photographs of the wild flowers. What we really ask is that you don't feed the ducks. Many people like to throw bread, but it makes them ill, so please don't.

script.speaker: Ruth
script.text: Finally, some events next month. We were going to run an astronomy night, but it's been cancelled because of the weather forecast. Instead we have a bat walk on the twelfth, and a photography workshop on the nineteenth. Pond-dipping is only in summer, and the craft market doesn't happen until December. Enjoy your visit.

parts.title: Supermarket packaging presentation
parts.contextVi: Hai sinh viên trao đổi với giảng viên về bài thuyết trình nhóm về bao bì nhựa trong siêu thị.

script.speaker: Dr Alvarez
script.text: Hello both, thanks for coming. You wanted to talk about your presentation on supermarket packaging. How's it going?

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Quite well, although we nearly chose a different topic. At first I suggested food waste, but Priya pointed out that almost every group in previous years has done it, so we went for plastic packaging instead.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: It also gives us a local angle. We're comparing three supermarkets in the town centre.

script.speaker: Dr Alvarez
script.text: Good. And how are you collecting your data? Last time you mentioned interviewing shoppers.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: That was the plan, but the store managers refused permission to stand outside their shops. So we've put a questionnaire online and we're sharing it through the university's social media.

script.speaker: Dr Alvarez
script.text: That's reasonable, but be careful. An online survey may attract mostly students, so your results might not represent ordinary shoppers. You need to mention that limitation in your talk.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: We did think of that. We're aiming for about two hundred responses, and we'll ask our families to share the link with their neighbours and friends as well.

script.speaker: Dr Alvarez
script.text: Good idea. Now, let's look at your sources. What have you found so far?

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: The council report looked ideal at first, because it has figures for every supermarket in the region.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: True, but it was published in twenty fourteen, so most of the packaging policies it describes have since changed.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Then there's the Greenfield Stores brochure about reducing plastic. It's full of impressive claims, but of course it only tells the company's side of the story.

script.speaker: Dr Alvarez
script.text: Yes, treat that with caution. What about academic sources?

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: There's a journal article on recycling rates. It's very thorough, but frankly the statistics are so complicated that we had to ask a lecturer to explain them to us.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: And we found a newspaper article saying supermarkets waste thousands of tonnes of plastic, but it gives no evidence for that figure, so we can't really use it.

script.speaker: Dr Alvarez
script.text: That's sensible. Now, the structure of the presentation. How long do you have?

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Fifteen minutes for the talk itself, then five minutes for questions, so twenty in total.

script.speaker: Dr Alvarez
script.text: Fine. For your conclusion, I'd suggest two things. First, a clear recommendation for the supermarkets, and second, an honest discussion of the weaknesses of your own research. You don't need to repeat all your survey results, and photographs belong earlier in the talk.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: That makes sense. When should we send you a draft of the slides?

script.speaker: Dr Alvarez
script.text: By next Friday, please. I'm at a conference on Thursday, so email it and I'll comment over the weekend. And do rehearse before the real thing, ideally in front of other students.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: We'll do that. I'll book a seminar room for Monday afternoon.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Thank you, Dr Alvarez. This has been really helpful.

script.speaker: Dr Alvarez
script.text: You're welcome. Good luck with the survey.

parts.title: Green roofs
parts.contextVi: Một bài giảng đại học về lịch sử, các loại hình, lợi ích và hạn chế của mái nhà xanh.

script.speaker: Dr Hartley
script.text: Today I'd like to talk about green roofs, that is, roofs deliberately covered with vegetation. Although they seem like a modern idea, the earliest examples are the turf roofs of traditional Scandinavian houses, where a layer of soil provided insulation against the cold. They were largely forgotten during the nineteenth century, until German engineers revived the concept in the nineteen sixties.

script.speaker: Dr Hartley
script.text: Modern green roofs come in two main types. Extensive roofs have only a thin layer of growing material, usually under fifteen centimetres, and are planted mainly with a hardy plant called sedum. They are light and cheap. Intensive roofs, by contrast, can support shrubs and even small trees, but they require much stronger structures underneath, as well as regular irrigation.

script.speaker: Dr Hartley
script.text: Let me now turn to the benefits, and the first is stormwater management. In a heavy rainstorm, a green roof can absorb up to eighty percent of the water that falls on it, which relieves the pressure on city drains and so reduces the risk of flooding. This is why a number of European cities have encouraged them.

script.speaker: Dr Hartley
script.text: The second benefit relates to temperature. Cities are warmer than the surrounding countryside, an effect known as the urban heat island. Plants cool the air through evaporation, and measurements in one Australian city showed that green roof surfaces were up to thirty degrees cooler than conventional ones on a summer afternoon.

script.speaker: Dr Hartley
script.text: Third, there is biodiversity. Even small roofs attract insects, and so-called brownfield roofs, which imitate abandoned industrial land, have attracted rare beetles, as well as nesting birds. In some cities, these roofs now act as stepping stones between parks that would otherwise be isolated.

script.speaker: Dr Hartley
script.text: However, there are drawbacks. The most obvious is cost, since installation can be three times that of a conventional roof. There is also the matter of maintenance, because weeds can damage the waterproof membrane. Some owners worry about leaks, but research suggests that properly installed roofs actually last longer, since the vegetation protects the roof from ultraviolet light.

script.speaker: Dr Hartley
script.text: Despite these concerns, several countries have made green roofs compulsory in certain cases. The best-known example is the Swiss city of Basel, where the regulations require all new flat roofs to be green. As a result, the city now has one of the highest proportions of green roofs in Europe.

script.speaker: Dr Hartley
script.text: To sum up, green roofs are an old idea that has been given new life by modern technology. Their value lies not in any single advantage but in the combination of water control, cooling and wildlife habitat. In the next session, we'll look at how their performance can be measured in practice.

script.text: Good morning, Harbourview Climbing Centre, Megan speaking. How can I help?

script.text: Yes, Thursday is fine. The first session at five thirty is already full, so I'd book you into the later one, at six thirty in the evening. It takes about ninety minutes.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: That's perfect. Is there anything I should bring?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Just comfortable sports clothes. We lend out climbing shoes for free during the induction. But do bring a padlock for your locker, because we provide the lockers but not the locks.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: OK, a padlock. I'll buy one on the way.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Now I'll ask a few questions for the form. How did you hear about us?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: My sister told me about you. She joined last year. I did see your advert on a bus too, but she's the reason I called.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Lovely. And what kind of climbing interests you most? We have bouldering, rope climbing and a fitness area.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: I'd like to try rope climbing eventually, but I've never done it. I'll start with bouldering, since I don't need a partner for that.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: That's sensible. Now, for membership, the standard one is fifty-two pounds a month and lets you come at any time. Off-peak is thirty-eight pounds, but only on weekdays before four o'clock. And there's a weekend-only one at thirty pounds.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: I finish work at half past five, and I'm busy on Saturdays, so off-peak and weekend-only are no good for me. I'll take the standard one.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Great. The joining fee is normally twenty pounds, but this month we're offering it at fifteen pounds.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Excellent. Thank you very much, Megan. I'll see you on Thursday.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Goodbye, Daniel. See you then.

parts.contextVi: Một người dẫn chương trình radio địa phương giới thiệu công viên mới sắp mở cửa trong thành phố.

script.speaker: Nadia
script.text: Welcome to the community slot on Greenline Radio. This week, the long-awaited Marlow Fields Park finally opens to the public on Saturday the twelfth of April. You may have seen the eleventh of April on some websites, but that's only a private preview for local councillors, so please don't turn up on Friday.

script.speaker: Nadia
script.text: Many people believe the city council paid for the whole project, but in fact most of the money, about seventy percent, came from a national lottery grant. The council paid for the playground, and a few local businesses donated the trees.

script.speaker: Nadia
script.text: The site has an interesting past. It was a tram depot for many years, and later a car factory, which closed in the nineteen nineties. For the last ten years or so, before building began, the land was used as a temporary car park, which is why the ground needed so much work.

script.speaker: Nadia
script.text: Now let me take you on a tour. When you come in through the East Gate, the first thing you'll see is a children's maze made of tall hedges. It's already popular with the families who've seen it growing. Further on, at the Lakeside, there's a wooden bird hide, where you can watch ducks and herons without disturbing them.

script.speaker: Nadia
script.text: Walk on to Orchard Corner, where old apple and pear trees have been kept, and you'll find several picnic shelters, so a shower won't spoil your lunch. If you're feeling energetic, climb up to the Hilltop, where artists have placed eight sculptures along a winding path, and the view over the city is wonderful.

script.speaker: Nadia
script.text: The last area is Old Station Square, by the West Gate, where a small café will serve hot drinks and cakes. An outdoor gym was planned for that area, but the council decided it was too expensive, and the bike repair stand has been postponed until next year.

script.speaker: Nadia
script.text: Opening hours: from April to September, the park is open from six in the morning until nine at night. In winter, the closing time was going to be five o'clock, but after requests from residents who walk home from work, the gates will now close at six.

script.speaker: Nadia
script.text: And finally, the opening weekend. On Saturday there'll be a guided history walk, and on Sunday morning children can join a tree planting session. We had hoped for live music too, but unfortunately the band has pulled out. Free bike checks won't start until May. See you there!

parts.title: Planning a presentation on food waste
parts.contextVi: Hai sinh viên thảo luận với giảng viên về bài thuyết trình cho môn học về phát triển bền vững.

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: Come in, both of you. So, you wanted to talk about your presentation for the sustainability module. Last week you were planning to look at plastic packaging, I think?

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: We were, but when we did a literature search, we found loads of recent studies already. We didn't think we could add anything new.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: Our first worry was that the topic was too broad, but the real problem was how much had been published. So we've switched to food waste.

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: That sounds sensible. What kind of data do you have in mind?

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: I thought we could ask supermarket managers, to get figures on how much they throw away.

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: Realistically, I doubt they'd agree, and you only have three weeks. But the campus café has weighed its waste every day for two years, and the manager is happy to share the records.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: That's much easier. Though I'd still like to look at households as well, because honestly I think families throw away far more food than shops do, and that's where the real problem is.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: Maybe, but the café figures give us numbers we can trust. Household waste is mostly guesswork.

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: You could add a short survey for the household side. Now, the format. The slot is twenty minutes altogether, but that includes five minutes of questions, so you have fifteen minutes to present.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: Fifteen, OK. For the slides, I think photographs of bins full of food would have more impact than graphs. People remember pictures.

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: Some, certainly, but I'd keep graphs for the main comparisons. And keep your introduction brief, no more than two minutes. Audiences lose patience if you take too long to reach your findings.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: We should rehearse with a timer, then. Last time we ran over by six minutes and lost marks.

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: Good idea. I read the draft outline you sent. The structure is clear, but the conclusion is weak. You describe the problem well, yet you don't suggest what the café could do differently.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: We can add some recommendations. We also ran a pilot survey last week, with fifty students.

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: How did it go?

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: Mostly fine, but nearly everyone who answered was under twenty-five, so we've hardly got any older people. And some questions confused people. Nobody understood what we meant by 'avoidable waste'.

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: Those are both fixable. I wouldn't worry about the length, ten questions is fine, and there's no need to translate it, since you're surveying English-speaking course members.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: So what should we do before the next tutorial?

script.speaker: Dr Marsh
script.text: Email me the revised outline by Friday if you can, but first of all go and meet the café manager, and ask which weeks' figures are the most reliable.

script.speaker: Priya
script.text: We'll do that tomorrow. Thanks, Dr Marsh.

parts.title: The history of glass
parts.contextVi: Một bài giảng đại học về lịch sử của thủy tinh, từ thủy tinh tự nhiên đến quy trình sản xuất hiện đại.

script.speaker: Dr Haldane
script.text: Good afternoon. Today's lecture is about glass, a material so familiar that we rarely think about where it came from. Let's begin with natural glass. When volcanic lava cools very quickly, it can solidify before crystals have time to form, and the best known example of this is obsidian. Early peoples all over the world used it to make sharp blades and, above all, arrowheads.

script.speaker: Dr Haldane
script.text: When was glass first made deliberately? Some older books say Egypt, and Egyptian glassmakers were certainly skilled, but the earliest evidence we have points to Mesopotamia, the region between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. Those early craftsmen could not blow glass. Instead they shaped small containers by wrapping soft glass around a core of clay, which was scraped out afterwards.

script.speaker: Dr Haldane
script.text: The real revolution came in the Roman period, with the invention of glassblowing in the first century before Christ. Blowing air through a tube allowed craftsmen to produce vessels far more quickly, and as a result glass became much cheaper, so that ordinary families, not only the wealthy, could afford cups and bottles.

script.speaker: Dr Haldane
script.text: The Romans also produced the first window glass, but it was thick and cloudy. Interestingly, the earliest windows were not installed in homes at all, but in bathhouses, where they helped to keep the heat in while still letting some light through.

script.speaker: Dr Haldane
script.text: Let's jump forward to the Middle Ages, when Venice became the glass capital of Europe. In the thirteenth century, the city ordered its glassmakers to move to the island of Murano. The official reason was the danger of fire, since furnaces burned day and night in a city of wooden buildings, although many historians suspect the rulers also wanted to protect their trade secrets.

script.speaker: Dr Haldane
script.text: In the seventeenth century, the English maker George Ravenscroft transformed the industry. By adding lead oxide to the mixture, he produced a heavy, brilliant glass which we still call lead crystal. It was softer to cut and decorate, and it quickly became fashionable across Europe.

script.speaker: Dr Haldane
script.text: The next major change came in the nineteen fifties, when Alastair Pilkington developed the float process. Molten glass is poured onto a bath of liquid tin, and because tin is so dense and perfectly level, the glass spreads out into a flat, smooth sheet. Before this, large sheets had to be ground and polished by hand, which was slow and wasteful.

script.speaker: Dr Haldane
script.text: Finally, a word about sustainability. Glass is made from sand, soda ash and limestone, all of them abundant, and unlike many materials it can be recycled endlessly without any loss of quality. Yet in many countries only a fraction of bottles is collected. Next week, we'll turn to metals and ask a similar question.

script.text: There was one with a blue front door in the photographs on your home page. I think it was called Heron Cottage. No, sorry, I've got the page open in front of me now. It's Kestrel Cottage.

script.text: Ah yes, Kestrel Cottage. That's one of our most popular properties. Heron Cottage is a different one, in the next village, and it's quite a lot smaller. Kestrel is in the village of Lanbury, and it's about ten minutes' walk from the beach.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: That sounds just right. There will be five of us, with three children, and the youngest is only four, so I'd like to know that it's safe for small children.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: It sleeps six, in three bedrooms, and the garden is completely fenced, so that's no problem. When were you hoping to arrive?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: We were thinking of the twelfth of June, because the children finish school the day before.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: I'm afraid that week is already booked. All our cottages change over on a Saturday, and the next free week at Kestrel starts on the nineteenth of June. After that, the next one is the twenty-sixth.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: The nineteenth is fine for us, thank you. We'd like to stay for seven nights.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: Good. Now, you'll want to know the price. The brochure says five hundred and twenty pounds a week, but that was last year's price, and it has been reduced. For a week in June it's four hundred and eighty pounds. In July and August it goes up to six hundred and fifty.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: That's well within our budget. Is there anything else we have to pay when we book?

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: We take a deposit of one hundred pounds, which is returned to you within two weeks after your stay, as long as there's no damage. The rest of the payment is due six weeks before you arrive.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: That's fine. And what about bed linen and towels? Do we need to bring our own?

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: No, they're included in the price, and so is electricity. But there are a few optional extras. You can order firewood for the stove, at twelve pounds a basket, or you can hire a rowing boat from the harbour for thirty pounds a day.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Oh, a boat sounds wonderful. The older children would love it.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: It's very popular, but I should mention that the life jackets are only available for children aged eight and over, so your youngest wouldn't be able to go out.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Ah, in that case I'll leave the boat. It wouldn't be fair on him. But we'll definitely take the firewood, because the evenings can be chilly by the sea.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: I'll add that to your enquiry. Now, about the keys. Normally guests collect them from our office in the High Street, but we close at four o'clock on Saturdays.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: We probably won't get there until about six.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: In that case there's an easy solution. There's a key safe on the wall by the back door of the cottage. We'll text you the code a few days before you travel, and you can let yourselves in.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: That sounds ideal. That's much better than rushing.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: Right, I think that's everything. We'll send you an email today with all the details and a booking form. How would you like to pay the deposit?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Could I do a bank transfer? I usually do it that way.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: We used to accept transfers, but they take several days to appear in our account. Most people pay by credit card over the phone, or you can send a cheque, but that takes even longer.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: I see. Well, I've got my card here, so I might as well do it now, if that's all right.

script.speaker: Helen
script.text: That's perfect. Let me put you through to my colleague, who will take the payment. Thank you so much for calling, Mr Morrow, and I hope you all enjoy your holiday.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Thank you very much for your help. Goodbye.

parts.title: Part 2 – Volunteer orientation at the city museum
parts.contextVi: Điều phối viên của bảo tàng thành phố chào đón các tình nguyện viên mới và giới thiệu ca làm việc cùng vị trí các phòng.

script.speaker: Grace
script.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Harbourgate City Museum. My name is Grace, and I coordinate the volunteer team. Thank you all for giving up your time. This morning I'll explain how your shifts work, show you where everything is, and tell you what we expect. We have had volunteers here since the nineteen sixties, and today there are more than ninety of you.

script.speaker: Grace
script.text: The museum is open from ten until five, and most volunteers work one shift a week. When I first advertised the role, I said shifts would last five hours, but several of you told me that was too tiring, so we changed it. Every shift is now four hours, either in the morning or in the afternoon, and you can swap with a colleague if you give us a few days' notice.

script.speaker: Grace
script.text: Some of you were hoping for a uniform, but we don't have one. You'll wear your own smart clothes, and the one thing you must always wear is the yellow name badge that you'll collect today. The green aprons belong to the shop and café staff, and the dark jackets belong to the security team, so please don't borrow either, however cold the galleries feel.

script.speaker: Grace
script.text: Many of you asked to guide school groups straight away, but that only comes after six months of experience. Most new volunteers begin at the information desk in the entrance hall, where you hand out floor plans, answer questions, and help people find the lifts and toilets. It's a good way to learn the building, and visitors always seem to ask the same ten questions.

script.speaker: Grace
script.text: Now I'll take you round the building in words, and you can follow on the plan in your folder. Let's start with where you'll spend your breaks. The volunteer lounge is on the first floor, beside the lift. Sorry, I'm wrong there, that's the staff office, which is always locked. The lounge is actually behind the café, through the blue door. There's a kettle, a fridge and plenty of comfortable chairs.

script.speaker: Grace
script.text: Back in the entrance hall, the coat and bag store is directly opposite the ticket desk. Please leave everything there except your phone and your water bottle, because large bags aren't allowed in the galleries. The shop is next to the main doors, on the left, and the café is straight ahead, but I'm sure you'll find those without any help from me.

script.speaker: Grace
script.text: If you go out through the side door and cross the courtyard garden, you'll come to the old stable block, which now houses our learning studio. That's where school groups do craft activities and handling sessions. It's the only space outside the main building, so wear a coat in winter. You can't miss it, because the green door has a large owl painted on it.

script.speaker: Grace
script.text: Downstairs in the basement is the conservation workshop. You won't be working there, and the door is kept locked, but now and then the conservators give a talk to the volunteers, and you'll be taken down in the goods lift. Please don't be tempted to go down alone, because some of the materials they use are hazardous.

script.speaker: Grace
script.text: If you go up the main staircase, the archive reading room is right at the top, on your left. Researchers and local history groups use it by appointment, and volunteers are sometimes asked to escort them. It was our library until last year, so you may still see people carrying boxes of old photographs and maps along the landing.

script.speaker: Grace
script.text: The first aid room is also on the first floor, but it's beside the lift, quite near the staff office I mentioned earlier. Our trained first aiders are listed on the noticeboard in the lounge. If a visitor feels unwell, stay with them, call a first aider on your radio, and never try to move anyone yourself.

script.speaker: Grace
script.text: Now, what happens at the start of every shift? First, you sign the register at the staff entrance, in case of a fire. Second, you collect a radio from reception, so that security can reach you. Some people think you should check the emergency exits, but security does that before we open. There's also a noticeboard with daily news, but I'll email you a summary, so you needn't read it.

script.speaker: Grace
script.text: Finally, a few words about the benefits. You'll get a free lunch voucher for the café after each shift, a discount in the shop, and an invitation to our summer party in the courtyard garden. We also run a monthly talk by a curator, which is a lovely chance to hear about objects normally kept in storage.

script.speaker: Grace
script.text: That's all from me for now. In a moment, my colleague Hassan will hand out your folders and name badges, and then we'll walk through the galleries together so you can see the building properly. Please ask questions at any time, because nobody remembers everything on the first day. Thank you again, and welcome to the team.

parts.title: Part 3 – Research project on urban noise
parts.contextVi: Hai sinh viên thảo luận với giảng viên về đề tài nghiên cứu tiếng ồn đô thị, gồm khu vực khảo sát và phương pháp thu thập dữ liệu.

script.speaker: Dr Ellis
script.text: Come in, both of you, and sit down. Right, I've read your project outline on urban noise, and I'd like to hear how you're feeling about it before we talk about method.

script.speaker: Sana
script.text: Honestly, quite excited. I grew up beside a railway line, so I assumed that was the reason I'd always been interested in noise. But actually, it was an article I read last year about traffic noise and children's sleep that made me want to investigate it properly.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: And I got involved mainly because Sana kept talking about it in the canteen. But I do like the idea of measuring something that everybody complains about without really knowing how loud it is.

script.speaker: Dr Ellis
script.text: Good. Now, my main concern with the outline is the aim. At the moment it says you'll investigate noise pollution in the city, which is far too broad for a project of this size. The topic itself is fine. A few students have looked at noise before, but your angle is new, and your timetable looks sensible.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: We were afraid you'd say that. We thought we could cover the whole centre, but when Sana drew up a map, it had about forty streets on it.

script.speaker: Sana
script.text: Which is impossible. So I suggested choosing one area. The streets around the railway station are the obvious choice, because they're the noisiest, but the council has already done several studies there.

script.speaker: Dr Ellis
script.text: Exactly, and you'd struggle to add anything new. What about somewhere with a mixture of noise sources?

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: What about the Fernley market area? There are stalls, buskers, early morning deliveries and a bus route, and people actually live in flats above the shops.

script.speaker: Dr Ellis
script.text: That sounds ideal. The residential streets beside the ring road would work too, but traffic would dominate everything you measured. I'd go with the market.

script.speaker: Sana
script.text: Then that's decided. The market it is.

script.speaker: Dr Ellis
script.text: Now, equipment. The department has two professional sound level meters that you can borrow. They're accurate, but you must calibrate them before every session, otherwise your readings will slowly drift, and you won't be able to defend them in your report.

script.speaker: Sana
script.text: We'd also thought of using phone apps, because they're free and we'd all have one with us.

script.speaker: Dr Ellis
script.text: For a pilot, that's fine. You could test where to put the meters and how long to record. But I wouldn't use them for your main data, because the microphones vary so much between phones.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: What about a questionnaire for residents? We wanted to ask how much the noise bothers them.

script.speaker: Dr Ellis
script.text: It's a worthwhile idea, but remember that if you ask people about their health or their sleep, you need approval from the ethics committee, and that can take several weeks. So you'd need to submit your form very soon.

script.speaker: Sana
script.text: And what about recording through the night? Callum thinks it would be pointless, because nothing happens after midnight except deliveries.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: That isn't what I said. I said it would be expensive, because we'd need weatherproof equipment and somewhere safe to leave it.

script.speaker: Dr Ellis
script.text: Callum's right about the cost. But overnight data is very reliable, because nobody disturbs the equipment, and the early deliveries are one of the main complaints. So it's costly, but worth one or two nights if you can borrow a unit.

script.speaker: Sana
script.text: We also wanted to interview the café owners and stallholders about how noise affects their business.

script.speaker: Dr Ellis
script.text: Be careful there. People with a commercial interest tend to exaggerate the problem or play it down, depending on whether they like the buskers. You can certainly use them, but you must treat what they say as biased.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: Finally, the council keeps records of noise complaints. We could use those to see when problems happen.

script.speaker: Dr Ellis
script.text: Yes, and that data is free, because they publish it online every quarter. You don't need to collect anything yourselves. Just download the figures for the market area.

script.speaker: Sana
script.text: That's helpful. It sounds like we've got plenty to work with.

script.speaker: Dr Ellis
script.text: You do. Now, thinking ahead to the report, what would you like to include apart from the data tables?

script.speaker: Sana
script.text: I'd love to have a map showing the noise levels at different spots, coloured from quiet to loud. People find those very easy to understand.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: I was thinking of a comparison with another city, perhaps Rotterdam, but I suppose that would take far too long to research.

script.speaker: Dr Ellis
script.text: It would. Stick to your own area. And what about the health side?

script.speaker: Sana
script.text: I'd like a section on how noise affects residents' health, but we're not medical students, so we'd be on thin ice.

script.speaker: Dr Ellis
script.text: Agreed, leave that to the specialists. As for background reading, a short review of earlier studies in your introduction is enough, not a whole chapter. What I would like to see is a final section with recommendations for the council. That's where you show your own thinking.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: Right. Then a map and a set of recommendations. We could suggest quieter delivery hours, for example, or limits on where buskers can stand.

script.speaker: Dr Ellis
script.text: Good, that's the kind of practical idea I mean. Now, let's look at your schedule for the next month, and work out when you can book those meters.

script.speaker: Sana
script.text: I'll check the department diary this afternoon, and then we can come back to you tomorrow.

script.speaker: Dr Ellis
script.text: Perfect. Send me an email as soon as you've done it, and well done, both of you. This is a much stronger plan than the first one.

parts.title: Part 4 – Bioluminescence in the ocean
parts.contextVi: Một bài giảng đại học về hiện tượng sinh vật biển tự phát sáng, chức năng của nó và các ứng dụng của con người.

script.speaker: Dr Lindqvist
script.text: Good afternoon. Today I want to talk about one of the most spectacular phenomena in the oceans, bioluminescence, which simply means light produced by living organisms. It is astonishingly common. Some estimates suggest that around three quarters of the animals living in open water below a few hundred metres can make their own light, which makes it far more widespread than most people imagine.

script.speaker: Dr Lindqvist
script.text: Chemically, the process is quite simple in principle. A molecule called luciferin reacts with oxygen, and the reaction is sped up by an enzyme. Many students assume that the enzyme is also called luciferin, but it is not. The enzyme is known as luciferase, and different species have evolved different versions of both molecules, which is why the light varies from one animal to another.

script.speaker: Dr Lindqvist
script.text: One feature stands out when you look at the colour of this light. Most of it is blue, sometimes with a slight tinge of green, and you might expect some of it to be red or yellow. Blue light has the wavelength that travels furthest through seawater, while red light is absorbed within a few metres of the surface. Evolution has simply favoured the colour that can actually be seen.

script.speaker: Dr Lindqvist
script.text: Now, why do animals bother? The first function is camouflage. In the twilight zone, predators look upwards and see the faint sunlight, so any animal swimming above them appears as a dark outline. Hatchetfish and some squid solve this by producing light from organs on their undersides. This is called counter-illumination, and it removes the animal's shadow.

script.speaker: Dr Lindqvist
script.text: A second function is defence. When a deep-sea shrimp is attacked, it releases a glowing cloud into the water, rather like an octopus uses ink, and it swims away in the dark while the predator is distracted. Other species, such as certain jellyfish, flash dramatically, so that a larger predator is attracted to the scene. This is known as the burglar alarm effect.

script.speaker: Dr Lindqvist
script.text: Light can also be used offensively. The best known example is the anglerfish, which has a long spine growing from its head, with a glowing tip full of bacteria. Small fish are attracted to it, assuming it is food, and swim close enough to be swallowed. The unlucky prey never sees the mouth until it is too late.

script.speaker: Dr Lindqvist
script.text: The fourth function is communication. In the Caribbean there are tiny crustaceans called sea fireflies. At certain times after sunset, the males release a pattern of glowing droplets as they swim upwards, leaving a vertical line of light. Each species uses a different rhythm, so females know which males to approach. Divers describe these lines as trails of light.

script.speaker: Dr Lindqvist
script.text: Most of us have seen photographs of glowing waves along a beach at night. The light comes from microscopic algae called dinoflagellates. They flash whenever the water around them is disturbed, so a breaking wave, a swimming fish or an oar will set them off. Biologists believe that this movement startles the small grazers that would otherwise eat the algae.

script.speaker: Dr Lindqvist
script.text: Sometimes the effect happens on an enormous scale. Sailors have reported what they call milky seas, in which the ocean glows evenly for hundreds of square kilometres. For a long time these accounts were treated as legend, but in the early two thousands, satellite sensors finally confirmed one, and researchers now believe that glowing bacteria are responsible.

script.speaker: Dr Lindqvist
script.text: Let me turn to what humans have done with all this. In medicine, researchers have inserted luciferase genes into bacteria, so that they can follow the progress of an infection inside laboratory animals. The infection lights up, and the scientists need not operate, so far fewer animals are needed. The same idea has since been adapted for testing new drugs, which saves enormous amounts of time.

script.speaker: Dr Lindqvist
script.text: There are military applications too. During the Second World War, bioluminescence was a real danger for ships at night. A vessel moving through plankton-rich water leaves a glowing wake, which an enemy aircraft could follow straight back to the ship. Navies still study the phenomenon today, and some modern ships have special designs to reduce the disturbance that makes the water glow.

script.speaker: Dr Lindqvist
script.text: Which brings me to the deep ocean itself, and the problem of studying animals that react to light. When the first submersibles went down, their bright white lamps made animals flee or flash in panic. Researchers then switched to red light, which most deep-sea animals cannot see, because, as I said earlier, red is absorbed so quickly in seawater that they never evolved to detect it.

script.speaker: Dr Lindqvist
script.text: Another approach is to use cameras that are sensitive to almost no light at all. A famous example was a system called the Eye-in-the-Sea, which was lowered into the dark with a dim lure that imitated the flash of a jellyfish. It attracted a giant squid, an animal that had never been filmed in its natural habitat before. This was in two thousand twelve.

script.speaker: Dr Lindqvist
script.text: To sum up, bioluminescence is not a curiosity. It is one of the main ways that life communicates, hunts and hides in the largest habitat on the planet. Next week, we'll look at the chemistry of fluorescence, which is often confused with bioluminescence, and I'll explain why the famous green protein from jellyfish belongs in a different category.

parts.title: Joining a community choir
parts.contextVi: Một người đàn ông mới chuyển đến gọi điện cho nhân viên của dàn hợp xướng cộng đồng để đăng ký tham gia.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Good morning, Riverside Community Choir, Megan speaking. How can I help you?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Oh, hello. My name's Daniel. I've just moved to the area and I'd really love to join a choir. I saw that you take new members this month, is that right?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Yes, that's right. We have a new term starting in two weeks, and we always welcome beginners. Let me take a few details first, if that's all right. Could I have your full name, please?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Sure. It's Daniel Hayley.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Could you spell the surname for me?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Of course. That's H, A, Y, L, E, Y. Most people write it with an I in the middle, but mine doesn't have one, so it catches everybody out.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Thanks, Daniel, I've got that. And what's the best phone number to reach you on? We send a text message reminder before each rehearsal.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: My mobile is oh seven seven one, three five two, eight eight four.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Let me read that back to you. Oh seven seven one, three five two, eight eight four. Is that correct?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Yes, perfect. That's the one I use all the time.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Lovely. Now, do you know what sort of voice you have? We have four sections in the choir, and we're a bit short of men at the moment.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Well, at school I sang bass, but my voice has changed a lot since then. These days I can reach the higher notes quite easily, so I think I'm a tenor now.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: That's good news, because we really need more tenors. You can always try both parts at the first rehearsal, and the conductor will move you if necessary.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: That sounds sensible. And when do you rehearse? I work during the day, so I can only come in the evening.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: It's every Thursday evening. People usually arrive from seven o'clock for a cup of tea and a chat, but the singing itself starts at seven thirty and we finish at nine thirty.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Seven thirty is fine for me. Is the rehearsal in the town centre? I don't have a car yet, so I'll be walking or taking the bus.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: It's at Marlow Hall, which is just behind the railway station, so it's very easy to reach. We used to use the church hall, but it was too small, so we moved last year.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Marlow Hall, I'll find it. And how much does it cost to join?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: The fee is thirty-five pounds a term for students and retired people. For everyone else it's forty-two pounds, and that includes all your music and a printed folder.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: I'm working full time, so I'll be paying the forty-two pounds. Can I pay on the first night, or do I need to send something in advance?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: You can pay on the first night, cash or card, whichever you prefer. Now, we have a concert at the end of term. It's the nineteenth of December, in the cathedral. Some members think it's the twenty-first, but that was the date last year.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: The nineteenth, I'll write that down. That's very soon, though. Do new members really perform in the concert, or do they just come along and listen the first time?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Everyone sings. We choose easy songs for the winter concert, mostly folk tunes and a few carols, and the conductor makes sure that newer members stand next to more experienced singers.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: That's reassuring. Do I have to do an audition before I can join?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Not at all. Years ago there was a proper audition in front of a panel, which put a lot of people off, but now it's just a five-minute chat with the conductor. She asks you to sing a simple scale so that she knows where to place you. Nobody is ever turned away.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Good, that's a relief. What should I bring on the first night?

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Some people bring their own sheet music, but there's no need, as we give you a folder. The most useful thing is a pencil, because the conductor changes the markings all the time. Oh, and please don't record anything on your phone. That's a firm rule.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: A pencil, and no recordings. Understood.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: One last thing, just for our records. How did you hear about the choir? Was it through our website?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: I did look at your website, but that was afterwards. My neighbour mentioned the choir a few weeks ago, though I didn't really think about it until I saw your poster in the library yesterday. That's what made me pick up the phone.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Wonderful, so I'll put down the poster. Well, Daniel, we're delighted to have you, and we look forward to seeing you on Thursday week.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Thank you very much, Megan. I'm already looking forward to it. See you then. Goodbye.

script.speaker: Megan
script.text: Goodbye, Daniel. Take care.

questions.explain: Daniel đánh vần họ: "H, A, Y, L, E, Y" nên họ là Hayley.

parts.title: Harbourside Food and Music Weekend
parts.contextVi: Một người dẫn chương trình radio giới thiệu cho thính giả lễ hội ẩm thực và âm nhạc cuối tuần ở bến cảng.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Hello and welcome to Weekend Watch, your guide to what's on in the city. I'm Tom Garrick, and today I'm taking you through the Harbourside Food and Music Weekend, which starts this Friday evening and runs until Sunday night. It's a huge celebration of local cooking and live music, and this year it's bigger than ever, with more than sixty stalls and eleven bands.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: First, getting there. Many of you will want to drive, but please don't. The harbour car park is closed for repairs all month, and the streets nearby fill up very quickly. Some people have suggested using the ferry from Northside, and it does stop close to the site, but it only runs once an hour. Your best option is the free shuttle bus from the railway station, which leaves every ten minutes.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Now, tickets. Entry on Friday is free for everyone after five o'clock, but on Saturday and Sunday you'll need a day pass. Adults pay twelve pounds, and children under twelve come in free, as long as they're with an adult. You can buy passes at the gate, though the organisers recommend booking online, because it's cheaper and the queues on Saturday morning can be very long.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: So what's new this year? Last year's most popular event was the cooking contest, and that returns on Sunday, along with two extra bands on the main stage. But the big addition is the Lantern Market, which opens after dark on Saturday. It's a night market with over twenty stalls, all lit by hundreds of paper lanterns, and I think it's going to be the highlight of the whole weekend.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Let me now guide you around the site. If you have the festival plan in front of you, you'll see that everything is arranged around the old harbour in a big circle, and the seven main areas are labelled A to G. I'll walk you through the ones you'll most want to visit, starting with the entrance, so you can follow me on the map.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: As you come in from the bus stop, you'll arrive at Pier Square. This is where all the street food is, with stalls serving dishes from fourteen different countries, from Korean dumplings to Peruvian grilled chicken. Last year the stalls were along the Ropewalk, but they've been moved here to make more space, so please don't go looking for them in the old place.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Walk on past the fountain and you'll find the Orchard Garden, which is the place to take the family. Children can join workshops where they make their own bread, from mixing the dough to taking it home warm in a paper bag. They run every hour from ten, and a grown-up is welcome to help, though it's mostly the children who end up covered in flour.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: Next is the Old Boathouse, a lovely old building right by the water. Inside you can try regional cheeses and apple cider, and best of all, the tasting is free, thanks to the farmers who sponsor it. You might think it's a cooking area because of the delicious smells, but the chefs are in a different building, so don't expect to see any demonstrations there.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: And that other building is the Market Hall. This is where the cooking demonstrations take place, led by chefs from the best restaurants in the region. There are four sessions a day, each lasting forty minutes, and seats are limited, so I'd arrive early. The Saturday afternoon session with a famous pastry chef is expected to be especially busy, so try Sunday if you can.

script.speaker: Tom
script.text: If you'd like to sit down with a drink, head to the Quayside Steps. Have a great weekend, and enjoy the food and the music!

parts.contextVi: Hai sinh viên gặp giảng viên để xin ý kiến về bài thuyết trình về ảnh hưởng của mạng xã hội đến giấc ngủ.

script.speaker: Dr Reyes
script.text: Come in, both of you, and sit down. So, you wanted to talk about the presentation for the Health and Behaviour module. Remind me of your topic, and tell me how far you've got.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: Thanks, Dr Reyes. We're looking at the effects of social media on sleep, specifically among university students. We've done most of the reading, and we've run a small survey, so we'd like your opinion on our plan.

script.speaker: Dr Reyes
script.text: Good. What first gave you the idea? Was it that article in the student newspaper a few weeks ago?

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: Actually, I only read that afterwards. The idea came from your lecture last term, when you mentioned that most students check their phones within five minutes of waking up. Hannah and I both thought, that's us.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: Yes. I'd also considered doing something on exam stress, but that felt too general. Nobody had really tested sleep and scrolling in our own halls of residence, so we decided to try it.

script.speaker: Dr Reyes
script.text: Sensible. Tell me about the survey, then. How did it go?

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: We asked one hundred and twenty students in the halls to fill in a questionnaire about bedtime and screen use. The response was better than we expected, actually. Almost everyone we approached answered.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: The problem is accuracy. People had to estimate how long they spent on their phones each evening, and when we compared that with the screen time figures on the phones themselves, most students had guessed far too low.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: We piloted the questions on friends first, so confusing wording wasn't the issue. It's just that people don't like to admit how much time they spend online.

script.speaker: Dr Reyes
script.text: That's a well-known limitation of self-reported data. It doesn't make your survey worthless, but you must say so openly. Treat it as a point for your discussion section rather than an apology.

script.speaker: Dr Reyes
script.text: Now, let's talk about your title. At the moment it's Social Media and Sleep, which is far too wide for fifteen minutes. You could spend an hour on it. A narrower focus would help.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: We thought about adding Young People, but that's just as vague. How about Night-time Scrolling and Sleep Quality in University Students?

script.speaker: Dr Reyes
script.text: Much better. It isn't misleading, and it's not too technical either, just specific. Keep that. Now, I've read the draft outline you sent me, so let me go through it section by section.

script.speaker: Dr Reyes
script.text: Your introduction first. You spend nearly four minutes on background and definitions. Your audience are students, they know what social media is. One minute is plenty, so I'd cut it right down.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: That's fair. I wrote most of that, and I think I got carried away with the history of the platforms.

script.speaker: Dr Reyes
script.text: Then the survey results. You've got two long tables of figures on one slide, and nobody will read them. A simple bar chart showing bedtime against hours of use would make your point instantly.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: We could do that. I'd have made a graph already, but I wasn't sure which figures to use.

script.speaker: Dr Reyes
script.text: Use the averages for each group. Next is the research on blue light from screens. The studies you cite are from about fifteen years ago, and the field has moved on. Look for recent work, especially anything that disagrees with the older findings.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: Honestly, I was wondering whether we should drop that section entirely, because the evidence seems to be changing.

script.speaker: Dr Reyes
script.text: No, keep it, but update it. It's the most scientific part of your talk, and a good evaluation of changing evidence will impress the markers.

script.speaker: Dr Reyes
script.text: Then there are your two interviews with students about their night-time habits. At present they come near the end. I'd start with them, because a real story grabs the audience's attention, and then you can bring in the numbers.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: That makes sense. We could open with a short quotation from one of them, and then explain why we looked into it.

script.speaker: Dr Reyes
script.text: Exactly. Finally, your recommendations. Switching off notifications, keeping phones outside the bedroom, setting a screen curfew. They are practical and clearly explained, so I wouldn't touch them.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: I thought we might shorten that part, because it felt a bit obvious.

script.speaker: Dr Reyes
script.text: It isn't obvious to everyone, and it's what people will remember. Leave it as it is.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: And how long do we have, exactly? I thought the handbook said twenty minutes.

script.speaker: Dr Reyes
script.text: It did last year, but it's been reduced. You'll have fifteen minutes for the presentation, followed by five minutes of questions, and I'll stop you if you go over.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: Fifteen, then. That's another reason to shorten the introduction.

script.speaker: Dr Reyes
script.text: Right. Now, what are you going to do before next Thursday? I'd like to see some progress.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: We'll rework the slides along the lines you suggested and email them to you by Monday. Is that early enough for you to give us feedback?

script.speaker: Dr Reyes
script.text: That's perfect. I'd also like you to record yourselves practising the talk, and watch it back. It's uncomfortable, but you'll spot problems you'd never notice otherwise.

script.speaker: Liam
script.text: I could also contact the university sleep clinic and ask for an interview. They might give us a useful quotation.

script.speaker: Dr Reyes
script.text: It's a nice idea, but you really don't have the time before the deadline. Concentrate on the slides and the practice. And there's no need to rewrite the questionnaire, since you've already collected your data. Good luck, both of you.

parts.title: How honeybees navigate
parts.contextVi: Một giảng viên sinh học giảng về cách ong mật định hướng và tìm đường về tổ.

script.speaker: Dr Lindgren
script.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Today I want to look at one of the great puzzles of animal behaviour, namely how honeybees find their way. A forager may fly three kilometres from the hive, visit hundreds of flowers, and return in a straight line, with a brain smaller than a sesame seed. How does it do it? The answer, as we'll see, involves several systems working together.

script.speaker: Dr Lindgren
script.text: Let's begin with the most important cue. Some early naturalists believed that bees followed scent trails, and others suggested that they simply remembered the route. Neither is the main explanation. Bees use the position of the sun as a compass, and they compensate for its movement across the sky, because their internal clock tells them where the sun ought to be at any given time of day.

script.speaker: Dr Lindgren
script.text: Of course, the sun is not always visible. Yet bees still navigate on cloudy days, and that was a mystery for decades. We now know that their eyes can detect polarised light, a pattern created as sunlight is scattered by the atmosphere, which remains visible through thin cloud. Even a small patch of blue sky is enough for a bee to work out where the sun is.

script.speaker: Dr Lindgren
script.text: This brings us to the famous waggle dance, decoded by the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch, a Nobel Prize winner. Back at the hive, a forager dances on the vertical comb. The angle of the waggle run, measured from straight up, shows the direction of the food relative to the sun. The liveliness shows its quality, but the length of each waggle run indicates the distance.

script.speaker: Dr Lindgren
script.text: But how does a bee measure distance in the first place? Not by counting wingbeats, nor by estimating the energy it has used, as people once thought. The answer is that it measures how much the landscape appears to move past its eyes as it flies. Evidence came from a tunnel experiment by Australian researchers in the nineteen nineties, in which bees flew through a narrow tunnel to reach food.

script.speaker: Dr Lindgren
script.text: When the tunnel walls were lined with stripes, the bees reported distances far greater than the real ones when they danced, because the patterns made the world seem to rush past at high speed. When the walls were plain, they underestimated the distance. This also explains why bees are rarely seen crossing large stretches of calm water, where there is almost nothing visual to measure.

script.speaker: Dr Lindgren
script.text: Distance and direction are not the whole story, however. Young bees do not simply fly off into the unknown. Before their first trip they make short orientation flights, hovering in front of the hive and memorising the shapes of nearby trees, buildings and fences. Colour seems to matter far less than outline. These landmarks matter most in the final approach.

script.speaker: Dr Lindgren
script.text: There is also, so to speak, a sixth sense. The abdomens of bees contain tiny particles of iron, and there is evidence that they can detect the Earth's magnetic field. In experiments where bees were kept near strong magnets, their dances became disoriented. However, the magnetic sense is probably a back-up, used for example inside the dark hive, rather than a primary compass for long journeys.

script.speaker: Dr Lindgren
script.text: To follow bees outside the hive, scientists needed a way to track insects weighing less than a tenth of a gram. Cameras proved useless over long distances, so the solution was harmonic radar. Researchers glued tiny transmitters, lighter than a grain of rice, to the backs of foragers, and a radar unit then followed their flights across open fields, producing detailed maps of every turn and pause.

script.speaker: Dr Lindgren
script.text: One striking experiment used this technique. Bees captured as they left the hive were released at an unfamiliar site several hundred metres away. Instead of flying randomly, many first flew the direction they would have taken from the hive, then turned and flew straight home. This suggests that bees may hold a mental map of their surroundings, rather than merely following fixed steps.

script.speaker: Dr Lindgren
script.text: Not everyone agrees, though. Critics argue that a collection of simple rules, such as head for the hive when you see this particular landmark, could produce the same behaviour without any true map. The debate is still running, and a decisive experiment has been hard to design, partly because bees are so small and so easily disturbed by the equipment attached to them.

script.speaker: Dr Lindgren
script.text: Why does all this matter? Because in recent decades many colonies have declined. Disease and the loss of habitat both play a part, yet one factor stands out. Studies show that bees exposed to certain pesticides lose their way, and many foragers never return to the hive. Even doses too small to kill them damage their memory, which is exactly what navigation depends on.

script.speaker: Dr Lindgren
script.text: Bear in mind that most of this work was done on one species in open country, and bees living in dense forest or crowded cities may rely on rather different cues.

script.speaker: Dr Lindgren
script.text: So, to summarise. Bees combine a sun compass, polarised light, a measure of distance from the flow of the landscape, learned landmarks and possibly a map, and each system acts as a back-up when another fails. Next week we'll turn to how colonies make collective decisions. Please read the two chapters on swarm behaviour before then. Thank you.
